attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: The 'genie' line describes the situation at the time: withdrawing Galactica's demo did not contain the technology. Reading it as an observation is faithful.

contract.note: Reading the metaphor as 'the technology stayed available after the demo was pulled' uses the reasons the speaker gave himself (open model and paper, ChatGPT). This is a fair, ordinary plain reading.

evidence.note: Dated report from Nov 2022. Meta paused only the demo and said the models stayed available to researchers. This is Meta's own statement, relayed by MIT Technology Review, not an independent check.
Dated 5 Dec 2022. ChatGPT was public and widely used during the period, so comparable capability was not contained.

reviews.rationale: Within the period, Meta withdrew only the Galactica demo and said its models stayed available, and ChatGPT was publicly and widely used. Nothing shows a full withdrawal or that no comparable model was available. The support condition is met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Will drop' is an unhedged forecast. 'Soon' gives no date. The baseline of under $500K for a custom-trained model is kept.

contract.note: The $500K baseline is MosaicML's cost to train a GPT-3-quality model from scratch. Counting fine-tuning an open model changes the metric: fine-tuning was always far cheaper, so a few-hundred-dollar fine-tune does not show the price fell. This stretches the reading in the speaker's favour. The two-year window is also the drafter's choice, not the speaker's.

evidence.note: Sept 2022 MosaicML figure of about $450K to train a GPT-3-quality model from scratch. Pre-post baseline only. Company disclosure.
June 2023 fine-tuning cost of a few hundred dollars. This measures fine-tuning, not from-scratch training, so it is not comparable with the baseline. Company disclosure.
MosaicML's own claim that MPT-30B beats GPT-3. Gives no from-scratch cost.
About $200K from scratch in May 2023, but for a model matched to LLaMA-7B, below the GPT-3-class baseline. Smaller models were already cheap in 2022, so this does not show a like-for-like drop.

reviews.rationale: Read like-for-like (from-scratch training at GPT-3 quality), the packet has no dated cost below about $450K. The packet itself notes the MPT-30B from-scratch cost is missing. The fine-tuning figure is a different metric, and MPT-7B is below the quality baseline. Nothing contradicts the forecast either. The evidence does not settle it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A rough comparative observation that ChatGPT could produce Galactica-like nonsense. 'More or less' is kept as a loose comparison.

contract.note: No measure was given. The rough reading (ChatGPT readily produced confident falsehoods and its filters could be bypassed) is the ordinary one and fits 'more or less just as capable'. It is not stretched.

evidence.note: Dated 5 Dec 2022. Reports ChatGPT's persistent plausible but false output.
Dated 5 Dec 2022. Stack Overflow found ChatGPT answers often wrong yet convincing and easy to produce in volume.
Dated 5 Dec 2022. ChatGPT's content filters were circumvented within hours, which undercuts the idea that refusals made it clearly less capable.
Describes the nonsense Galactica produced, which is the point of comparison.

reviews.rationale: Reports from the period show that in its first week ChatGPT readily produced confident, plausible falsehoods and that its filters were easily bypassed. That is comparable to what Galactica was criticised for. No head-to-head test exists, but the rough reading needs none, and nothing shows ChatGPT reliably avoided such output.
